extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political theology, ecclesiastical law, and church-state relations
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted standards and principles about who may make church law, how ecclesiastical officers were chosen and maintained in apostolic and early Christian practice, and the relation of civil sovereign power to pastoral authority. Useful for analysis of church–state authority, ordination practice, and historic revenue rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts of council not laws without civil sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: The Acts of Councell of the Apostles, were then no Laws, but Councells; much lesse are Laws the Acts of any other Doctors, or Councells since, if assembled without the Authority of the Civill Soveraign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Councils' decrees are not binding laws on Christians unless backed by civil sovereign authority; ecclesiastical councils sitting without civil legislative power cannot create laws obliging subjects under civil government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostolic burdens are conditions for salvation, not civil laws
rubrics_metrics.description: By the Burthen, which the Apostles might lay on such as they had converted, are not to be understood Laws, but Conditions, proposed to those that sought Salvation; which they might accept, or refuse at their own perill, without a new sin...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obligations imposed by apostles functioned as spiritual conditions for salvation rather than juridical civil duties; rejecting them risks condemnation but is not a civil sin punishable as disobedience under temporal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostles obliged to teach agreed doctrine among themselves only
rubrics_metrics.description: The Apostles, and Elders of that Councell, were obliged even by their entrance into it, to teach the Doctrine therein concluded, and decreed to be taught, so far forth, as no precedent Law, to which they were obliged to yeeld obedience, was to the contrary; but not that all other Christians should be obliged to observe, what they taught.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members of a council are bound to teach its decisions within limits of preexisting law, but council directives do not automatically bind the broader Christian population absent civil enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptures cannot be made civil law except by sovereign authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The Books of the New Testament, though most perfect Rules of Christian Doctrine, could not be made Laws by any other authority then that of Kings, or Soveraign Assemblies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even canonical scriptures become civilly enforceable only when a sovereign (king or assembly with legislative power) adopts them into law; ecclesiastical canonical status alone does not confer civil legal force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public liturgical mandates addressed only to ecclesiastical officers
rubrics_metrics.description: The first Councell for setling the Canonicall Scripture... Can. 59. which forbids the reading of other Books then those in the Churches; which is a Mandate that is not addressed to every Christian, but to those onely that had authority to read any publiquely in the Church; that is, to Ecclesiastiques onely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some canonical rules (e.g., prohibiting reading certain books publicly) are directives for those who hold public ecclesiastical office, not general obligations on all Christians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of magisteriall vs ministeriall ecclesiastical offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Of Ecclesiastical Officers in the time of the Apostles, some were Magisteriall, some Ministeriall. Magisteriall were the Offices of preaching... and of teaching the Rules of Faith and Manners to those that were converted. Ministeriall was the Office of Deacons, ... administration of the secular necessities of the Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify church offices by function: magisterial (teaching, sacraments, ministry of word) versus ministerial (serving tables, secular administration). This distinction informs who may perform doctrinal acts vs. practical services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostleship requires witness of the Resurrection
rubrics_metrics.description: This Testimony, was the specificall, and essentiall mark; whereby the Apostleship was distinguished ... necessary for an Apostle, either to have seen our Saviour after his Resurrection, or to have conversed with him before, and seen his works...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being an apostle carried an essential qualification: being a credible witness of Christ's resurrection (direct appearance or prior personal acquaintance and witnessing of his works). This is the standard for authentic apostolic office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congregational election and authorization of apostles and ministers
rubrics_metrics.description: Matthias Made Apostle By The Congregation... there were assembled together in Jerusalem about 120 Christians ... they appointed two... and caused lots to be drawn; ... the Lot fell on Matthias and he was numbered with the Apostles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates that apostles (e.g., Matthias) and later presbyters/pastors were chosen and authorized by the local congregation (assembly), often by lot or plurality suffrage, not solely by a single preexisting apostle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophets and evangelists as gifts, not permanent offices
rubrics_metrics.description: By the names of Evangelists and Prophets, is not signified any Office, but severall Gifts, by which severall men were profitable to the Church...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat gifts like prophecy and evangelism as charisms usable by different persons rather than fixed hierarchical offices; authorship of gospels or prophetic revelation did not by itself create a perpetual institutional office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordination of elders/presbyters via assembly plurality (cheirotonesantes)
rubrics_metrics.description: When they had Ordained them Elders by the Holding up of Hands in every Congregation... to ordain an Officer in any of the Cities, was no more but to bring the people together, to elect them by plurality of Votes...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early ordination practice involved the congregation electing elders by plurality (raising hands, ballots, etc.), with apostles presiding to declare and bless the election rather than unilaterally appointing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early bishops/elders/pastors were essentially the same office
rubrics_metrics.description: Bishop, Pastor, Elder, Doctor, ... were but so many divers names of the same Office in the time of the Apostles. For there was then no government by Coercion, but only by Doctrine, and Perswading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reading later hierarchical distinctions into earliest practice: titles denoted overlapping functions of oversight and teaching rather than coercive institutional ranks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deacons are ministers of the congregation; pastors ministers of Christ
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pastors of the Church, called 'The Ministers of the Word,' are Ministers of Christ, whose Word it is: But the Ministery of a Deacon ... is a service done to the Church, or Congregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify that deacons serve practical needs of the congregation (table service, revenues, buildings), while pastors/teachers serve Christ by ministering the Word — a distinction bearing on authority to administer certain rites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostolic laying on of hands as conferring Holy Ghost and signs
rubrics_metrics.description: it was necessary for the conferring of the Holy Ghost, that their Baptisme should be administred, or confirmed by a Minister of the Word, not by a Minister of the Church... those graces that were signs of the Holy Spirit... 'These signs follow them that beleeve in my Name; they shall cast out Devills; they shall speak with new tongues...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain spiritual gifts and the formal conferral of the Holy Ghost were tied to apostolic/minister-of-the-word imposition of hands; some ministrations (e.g., confirmation of Holy Spirit signs) required ordained ministers rather than deacons.

rubrics_metrics.name: First deacons chosen by congregation, not apostles
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the saying pleased the multitude, and they chose seven, &c.' ... that the first Deacons were chosen, not by the Apostles, but by a Congregation of the Disciples
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinforces the principle of congregational choice for ministerial roles in the apostolic church; apostles only presided and declared the election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Under Mosaic law, Levites' maintenance was public/civil revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: To the Tribe of Levi were assigned certain Cities... for their portion, they were to have the tenth of the fruits... the Priests for their maintenance had the tenth of that tenth, together with part of the oblations, and sacrifices... Gods inheritance, was their maintenance... the Right of Tythes, and Offerings was constituted by the Civill Power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tithes and priestly maintenance under the Mosaic order were public revenues: their right derived from the political order (God as King/Moses as lieutenant), not from voluntary benevolence as in early Christian practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers of the Gospel lived by voluntary benevolence before Constantine
rubrics_metrics.description: the maintenance of the Bishops, and Pastors of the Christian Church, was nothing but the voluntary contribution of them that had embraced their Doctrine. There was yet no mention of Tythes...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the apostolic and early post-apostolic period ministers subsisted on voluntary gifts, alms, and personal labour; institutionalized tithes arose later (post-Constantine) and depended on civil enactment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paul's 'live of the Gospel' implies congregational determination of maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: From which place may be inferred indeed, that the Pastors of the Church ought to be maintained by their flocks; but not that the Pastors were to determine, either the quantity, or the kind of their own allowance... Their allowance must needs therefore be determined, either by the gratitude, and liberality of every particular man of their flock, or by the whole Congregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While ministers have a right to support ('live of the Gospel'), the amount and manner of maintenance should be set by the congregation's voluntary liberality or congregation-wide agreement, not unilaterally by pastors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil sovereign's right to judge doctrine for peace and to appoint pastors
rubrics_metrics.description: the Right of Judging what Doctrines are fit for Peace, and to be taught the Subjects, is in all Common-wealths inseparably annexed ... to the Soveraign Power Civill ... Christian Kings are still the Supreme Pastors of their people, and have power to ordain what Pastors they please, to teach the Church, that is, to teach the People committed to their charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereigns retain authority to determine what religious doctrines may be taught within their realm for the sake of civil peace, and therefore possess the right to appoint or authorize pastors in their dominions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church elections within a commonwealth are acts of the sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: For in that he is a Christian, he allowes the Teaching; and in that he is the Soveraign (which is as much as to say, the Church by Representation,) the Teachers hee elects, are elected by the Church... when an Assembly of Christians choose their Pastor in a Christian Common-wealth, it is the Soveraign that electeth him, because tis done by his Authority;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local congregational elections take place under the sovereign's authority in a Christian commonwealth; thus an election is legally the act of the sovereign even if locally conducted by the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral authority of sovereign is de jure divino; others jure civili
rubrics_metrics.description: All Pastors, except the Supreme, execute their charges in the Right, that is by the Authority of the Civill Soveraign, that is, Jure Civili. But the King, and every other Soveraign executeth his Office of Supreme Pastor, by immediate Authority from God, that is to say, In Gods Right, or Jure Divino.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish legal bases: the sovereign's pastoral authority is asserted as divine in origin (de jure divino), whereas subordinate pastors hold authority by civil grant (jure civili); this has implications for the form of titles and mandates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bishops should acknowledge civil subjection in titles/mandates
rubrics_metrics.description: Bishops ought to say in the beginning of their Mandates, 'By the favour of the Kings Majesty, Bishop of such a Diocesse;' or as Civill Ministers, 'In his Majesties Name.' For in saying, Divina Providentia... they deny to have received their authority from the Civill State...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ecclesiastical officials are expected to frame their commissions as deriving from the sovereign's favour or name to acknowledge civil subjection and avoid undermining the unity/defense of the commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christian sovereigns possess power to perform sacraments and consecrate
rubrics_metrics.description: it seemeth that he hath also the Authority, not only to Preach ... but also to Baptize, and to Administer the Sacrament of the Lords Supper; and to Consecrate both Temples, and Pastors to Gods service; which most men deny; partly because they use not to do it;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sovereign's pastoral power extends, in principle, to sacramental and consecratory acts; practical non-performance is due to convenience and delegation, not because the sovereign lacks the authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imposition of hands is an ancient ceremony to designate and consecrate
rubrics_metrics.description: Imposition of Hands, was a most ancient publique ceremony ... designed, and made certain, the person, or other thing intended in a mans prayer, blessing, sacrifice, consecration, condemnation, or other speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While laying on of hands historically served as a visible means to designate persons/things in consecration and ordination, its antiquity and function do not necessarily make it the sole legal/ontological source of authority for sovereign acts of consecration.
